state.misconception_label: Adds when calculating volume instead of multiplying

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The volume of this cuboid is \( 30 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \) What length should replace the star? ![A cuboid, depth 2cm and height 3cm. The width is labelled with a star.](). I got \( 25 \mathrm{~cm} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's explore what might happen if you tried a different approach to this problem. What if you considered how the dimensions of the cuboid are related to each other when calculating the volume?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess the dimensions do relate to each other, but I'm still not sure how to use them together. I thought I just needed to add them up to get the volume. So, if I shouldn't add, what exactly should I do with the numbers?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let me ask you this: What would happen if you tried your method on a simpler version of the problem, like a cube with sides of length 2 cm?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively engages the misconception through a well-calibrated counterexample strategy that requires genuine reasoning, but the student's final turn shows they haven't yet grasped the correct operation (multiplication), only that addition might be wrong.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions without giving direct answers, and in Turn 3 employs a counterexample (simpler cube case) to help the student discover the flaw in their additive reasoning—a textbook application of the Socratic method.
